.. _scripts-craftrecipe:

craftRecipe
===========

:Soft Override: True

The 'craftRecipe' script block is used to define a crafting recipe, which allows players to craft items or tiles in the game based on the parent script block. For example, a craftRecipe defined inside a `module <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/module.html>`_ will be a recipe to craft an item usually, while when defined inside an `entity <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/entity.html>`_ it will be the building recipe for that entity.

A craftRecipe will usually require an `inputs <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/inputs.html>`_ and `outputs <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/outputs.html>`_ block. Other parameters are used to define properties of this recipe, such as the `time <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/craftrecipe.html#time>`_ it takes to craft or the `XP awarded <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/craftrecipe.html#xpaward>`_ for crafting it.

For example:

.. code-block:: java

   module yourModule /* or Base */
   {
       craftRecipe yourRecipeID
       {
           ...
       }
   }

Some methods to modify existing recipes are documented on the `wiki <https://pzwiki.net/wiki/CraftRecipe#Modifying_existing_recipes>`_.

To define a translation for this recipe, you need to create an entry in the translation file `Recipes.json <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/translations/translation_files.html#recipes>`_. The translation entry should be formatted like this:

.. code-block:: json

   {
     "yourRecipeID": "Your recipe"
   }

Notice how you shouldn't use the `module <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/module.html>`_ in the translation file key and only the craftRecipe ID.

Here's an example of a craftRecipe with some parameters defined:

.. code-block:: java

   craftRecipe SawLogs
   {
       timedAction = SawLogs,
       Time = 230,
       Tags = InHandCraft;CanBeDoneFromFloor,
       category = Carpentry,
       xpAward = Woodwork:5,
       inputs
       {
           item 1 [Base.Log] flags[Prop2],
           item 1 tags[Saw] mode:keep flags[MayDegradeLight;Prop1],
       }
       outputs
       {
           item 3 Base.Plank,
       }
   }

content.content:
.. attribute:: category
   :noindex:

:Type: translation

:Default: ``Miscellaneous``

The category under which the recipe will be listed in the crafting menu. Helps to organize and identify recipes in crafting menu. Your category should have a key with the suffix ``IGUI_CraftingCategories_`` in the `IG_UI.json <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/translations/translation_files.html#ig-ui>`_ translation file to be properly displayed in the crafting menu. For example:

.. code-block:: java

   category = MyCategory,

And in the translation file:

.. code-block:: json

   {
     "IGUI_CraftingCategories_MyCategory": "My Category"
   }


.. _scripts-craftrecipe-icon:

.. attribute:: Icon
.. attribute:: SkillRequired
   :noindex:

:Type: object (object: string->>integer, kv: ':', pairs: ';')

Specifies the skill level required to perform this crafting action. It should be formatted this way:

.. code-block:: java

   /* a single skill */
   skillRequired = <skill name>:<level>,

   /* multiple skills */
   skillRequired = <skill1 name>:<level>;<skill2 name>:<level>,

For the list of available skills, see the `wiki <https://pzwiki.net/wiki/CraftRecipe#Available_skills>`_.

For example:

.. code-block:: java

   skillRequired = Blacksmith:3;Tailoring:2,


.. _scripts-craftrecipe-tags:

.. attribute:: tags
   :noindex:

:Type: array (array of string, separator: ';')

:Required: True

Specifies specific conditions which need to be respected to craft this item. At least one crafting bench tag is necessary for the craft to be recognized, such as ``AnySurfaceCraft``. The syntax is as follows:

.. code-block:: java

   /* single tag */
   Tags = tag1,

   /* multiple tags */
   Tags = tag1;tag2;...,

For example:

.. code-block:: java

   Tags = InHandCraft;CanAlwaysBeResearched,

A crafting bench tag can be created by adding a `component CraftBench <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/component/component-craftbench.html>`_ to an `entity <https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/entity.html>`_ script, which can then be used in this tags parameter.

You can find a list of tags available on the `wiki <https://pzwiki.net/wiki/CraftRecipe#List_of_tags>`_.


.. _scripts-craftrecipe-time:

.. attribute:: time
   :noindex:

:Type: integer

:Default: ``50``

The time it takes to craft the item, not using a specific unit of time so refer to the vanilla recipes to get an idea of what value to use.

content.content: {{Navbar modding}} {{Page version|42.19.0}} {{About|creating custom sandbox options (modding)|an explanation of options in the 'sandbox' game mode|Custom Sandbox}} '''Sandbox options''' allow users to tweak how they want to experience the game, which mods can also utilize. In comparison to {{ll|ModOptions}}, these settings apply to every player, but like these, you have access to different types of options. They use {{ll|Scripts}} syntax. Mods sandbox options are defined in a file named sandbox-options.txt with the following folder structure: {{CodeSnip | code = 📁 media 📄 sandbox-options.txt }} {{Note|To get more information on the modding folder structure and the media folder, see the {{ll|Mod structure}} page.}} The file starts with the parameter VERSION = 1, which is used by the game to recognize which method needs to be used to read the sandbox option file. It's used by developers in case they change the way this file reads in future updates. Unless you know what you are doing, you shouldn't change this value. The rest of the file is a list of sandbox options, each defined by an [https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/option.html option] {{ll|Scripts}} file. All blocks will follow the following structure: {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = option ModName.OptionName { type = , ... page = , translation = _, } }} You can choose any name for ModName and OptionName without spaces, but it is usually your mod name and a logical option name for easier identification. Accessing the option value in Lua will be done with SandboxVars.ModName.OptionName. You can set pageName to a custom page name of your choosing to create new tabs in the Sandbox Options menu. == Option types == The type parameter defines the type of the option which replaces in the example code above. The following lists every type and their various parameters: {| class="wikitable theme-blue" ! Option type !! Description !! Parameters |- | boolean | Booleans are used for options that can be either true or false. | {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = type = boolean, default = , }} |- | integer | Integers are used for options that can be any whole number. | {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = type = integer, default = , min = , max = , }} |- | double | Doubles are used for options that can be any float number. | {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = type = double, default = , min = , max = , }} |- | string | Strings are used for options that can be any text. For an empty string by default, use default = ,. | {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = type = string, default = , }} |- | enum | Enums are used for options that can be one of a list of predefined values. | {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = type = enum, default = , numValues = , }} |} For example: {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = option MyMod.MyOption { type = boolean, default = true, page = MyPage, translation = MyMod_MyOption, } }} == Translations == You can also add {{ll|Translations}} for your options in the translation folder. This is also needed if you want to give your option a proper name in the game. Sandbox options are put in the following file: {{CodeSnip | code = 📁 media 📁 lua 📁 shared 📁 Translate 📁 📄 Sandbox.json }} The different sandbox options need extra parameters first: {{CodeSnip | lang = java | code = option ModName.OptionName { type = , .. _scripts-root-sandboxoptions: ROOT-SandboxOptions =================== :Soft Override: Unknown :Is Root: True :Root patterns: ``media\/sandbox-options\.txt$`` The root of a sandbox options file. The file should be stored in the following path: .. code-block:: 📁 media 📄 sandbox-options.txt You can find more information about sandbox options `here `_. Hierarchy --------- This block can have the following child blocks: - :ref:`option ` Parameters ---------- .. _scripts-root-sandboxoptions-version: .. attribute:: VERSION :noindex: :Type: Unknown :Required: True :Allowed values: ``1`` The version of the handler of the sandbox options. Keep this equal to 1.

content.content: type = , ... page = , translation = _, } }} Both and _ are used with the translation system to give a proper name to the option in the game. The is the name of the page where the option will be displayed in the game, while _ is the translation key for the option name. The translations are defined in the translation file with the following structure: {{CodeSnip | lang=json | code = { "Sandbox_": "The page name", "Sandbox__": "The option name", "Sandbox___tooltip": "This is the tooltip of the option." } }} It's important to note that the tooltip translation is optional, but it's recommended to add it for better understanding of the option. You can also use {{ll|ISRichTextPanel}} tags in the tooltip, which means you can add images and colors in the sandbox options but also have custom text formating. {{Note|type=warn|If you don't add the translation parameters, they can't appear in-game, but if the translation doesn't exist in the translation files, it will simply appear with the string in the translation parameters.}} === Enumeration translation === Enumeration options need to have their values translated in the translation file. The translation tag in the translation file for all values needs to be "Sandbox___option": "Enum name". For example: {{CodeSnip | lang=json | code = { "Sandbox___option1": "First value", "Sandbox___option2": "Second value" } }} == Sandbox options in the Lua == You can access the value of a sandbox option in Lua by using the SandboxVars table. The table is structured as follows: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local optionValue = SandboxVars.ModName.OptionName print(optionValue) -- This will print the value of OptionName }} Alternatively you can also access it by using: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = getSandboxOptions():getOptionByName("ModName.OptionName"):getValue() }} You can also modify the value of a sandbox option in Lua by using the setValue function: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local sandboxOptions = getSandboxOptions() sandboxOptions:getOptionByName("ModName.OptionName"):setValue(newValue) -- to have changes applies java side, use sandboxOptions:toLua() -- for server syncing, use sandboxOptions:sendToServer() }} {{Note|{{Code|toLua}} sends the option changes to the Java, and not the Lua.}} == External links == * [https://github.com/demiurgeQuantified/PZModdingGuides/blob/main/guides/SandboxOptions.md Sandbox Options guide] by Albion == Navigation == {{Navbox modding}} {{ll|Category:Modding guides}} {{ll|Category:Scripts}} {{Navbar modding}} {{Page version|42.21.0}} '''Load order''' in {{ll|Modding}} is often presented as important when it really isn't as issues very rarely arise from wrong load orders. The basic of it is that load order doesn't matter if no mods override each others or the same vanilla files. Making sure mods don't override the same thing can be complex when you don't know much about modding, for this you can simply try to compare mods you activate and think if they replace the same features of the game, or if two mods do the same thing or impact the same features. The best way would be to check the {{ll|Mod structure#Online workshop folder|mod files}} but this can prove impossible when you have to compare with hundreds if not thousands of other mods. If you think a mod may clash with your mod, you'd be interested to check their files however. == Mapping == {{ll|Mapping|Maps}} are the most at risk of load order but as long as they don't share {{ll|Mapping#Cells|cells}}, there won't be any particular need for load order. Tiles depend on if another mod replaces another tile mod tiles. But even then load order cannot fix conflicts between maps and one of the two will have broken elements eitherway, you can't do anything about it but move those maps elsewhere (which isn't a solution either). Tiles can have their [https://pz-wiki-modding.github.io/PZ-API-Docs/scripts/root_files/modinfo.html#scripts-root-modinfo-tiledef tiledef ID] clash. but to reduce this risk you can chose an ID that is not yet documented in {{ll|Tiledefs used by mods}}, which lists a large amount of tiledef IDs already used. When it comes to {{ll|Mapping#Cells|cells}} being shared between map mods, there isn't a data base currently of already shared map cells. Tools like {{ll|Map Mod Manager}} and {{ll|PZ Map Analyser}} allows you to verify conflicts between map mods. == Lua and Scripts == {{ll|Lua (API)|Lua}} and {{ll|Scripts}} mods should almost never depend on load order as it is extremely easy to not have them clash with others. When they clash with each others it is either one of the following cases: # The modder didn't put his files at unique relative paths (see {{ll|Lua (API)#Folder structure}} and {{ll|Scripts#Folder structure}}) # They are overriding files they don't have to (see {{ll|Scripts#Soft overrides|Scripts soft overrides}} and {{ll|Lua (language)#Decoration|Lua decorations}}) # They had no choice but overwrite a file In the majority of cases you will be in scenario 1 or 2 and it is very easy to prevent these situations. === File overwrites === File overwrites can often be accidental where you don't realize your files will clash with other mods. Files in the media/lua and media/scripts folder will overwrite files with the same relative path to media. Mods which are loaded last (below) another one will overwrite that other mod files. For example: {{CodeSnip | lang = bash | code = # first mod 📁 media 📁 lua 📁 shared 📄 main.lua # second mod 📁 media 📁 lua 📁 shared 📄 main.lua # this will overwrite the first mod files }} {{Note|Files being in the {{ll|Mod structure#Common and versioning folders|common or versioning folders}} don't matter, only the currently loaded files of the mods can clash with each others. }} To prevent this, the solution is very easy: simply make a subfolder named after your mod that will contain all your mod files. {{CodeSnip | lang = bash | code = # first mod 📁 media 📁 lua 📁 client 📁 server 📁 shared 📁 MyFirstMod 📄 main.lua # second mod 📁 media 📁 lua 📁 client 📁 server 📁 shared 📁 MySecondMod 📄 main.lua # this will overwrite the first mod files }} For {{ll|Lua (API)|Lua}} mods, the client, server and shared folders (see {{ll|Lua (API)#Folder structure}}) will not clash between each others. Simply remember it is the relative path '''to the media folder''' that matters for file clashes for Lua and Scripts. For {{ll|Scripts}} mods, overwriting the vanilla files is almost completely not a solution but they are automatically generated and items are almost all in the same files. The good news is that you should not have to do that thanks to methods to modify existing scripts such as {{ll|Scripts#Soft overrides|soft overrides}} or in some cases documented methods to modify scripts from the Lua (see {{ll|Item (scripts)#Modifying existing item definitions}} and {{ll|CraftRecipe#Modifying existing recipes}}). == Textures, animations and models == {{Stub|This section needs more information how texture, animation and model files clash with each others between mods.}}

content.content: {{Navbar modding}} {{Page version|42.21.0}} {{About|the Lua API|a guide to learn how to code with Lua|Lua (language)}} Project Zomboid allows modders to program functionalities via a {{ll|Java}} implementation of '''{{ll|Lua (language)|Lua}}''' called Kahlua, which enables Lua scripts to run within Java programs. It bases itself on [https://www.lua.org/manual/5.1/ Lua 5.1] with a few differences and allows the use of exposed Java class and methods from Lua scripts. It is highly suggested to take note of the {{ll|JavaDocs}} and possibly {{ll|Decompiling game code|decompiling the game code}} to make your life easier when it comes to finding functions and understanding their inner working to more easily manipulate the game's Lua. Alternatively, an unofficial project called {{ll|LuaDocs}} acts like a JavaDocs but for the Lua API. {{ll|Java}} modding also exists and is a more powerful way to mod the game, by reducing the limitations to the minimum. However, it is more complex and has its own major drawbacks. == Video guide == {{Video |id=FGbyLGLmxes |image=PZ Modding Guides - Lua API, Java-Lua interface - thumbnail.png |name=PZ Modding Guides - Lua API, Java-Lua interface }} == How do Java classes work in the Lua API == Lua acts as a bridge to the Java, thanks to Project Zomboid's API. Every time you try to run functions on a Java object from Lua, there are more operations happening than simply running a Lua function on a Lua object, which is also the source of performance impacts (see {{ll|Mod optimization}}). There are many ways to access the various class objects in the game, sometimes easy and sometimes not so easy. The usual way is to utilize {{ll|Lua event}}s which will output the various class objects they refer to. Take for example {{ll|OnZombieUpdate}} which runs for every single zombies and every zombie update tick: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local function OnZombieUpdate(zombie) -- Your code here end Events.OnZombieUpdate.Add(OnZombieUpdate) }} In this case, the variable {{Code|zombie}} is an [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/characters/IsoZombie.html IsoZombie] with various methods that can be used on it. Sometimes it involves creating one yourself with a {{ll|#Constructor}} or directly retrieving the list of objects. Most classes can have multiple instances, like in the case of IsoZombie. === Parent and subclasses === [[File:Lua (API) - subclasses.png|class=logo-dark|right|500px|The parent and subclass relationship between Java classes with IsoZombie as an example.]] All Java classes are a subclass to another class, and might also be the parent to subclasses. On the side here, you can see a representation of this relationship, with an example of the IsoZombie class and its parent and subclasses. Subclasses inherit all the public and protected methods and fields from their parent class, while also having their own unique methods and fields, possibly overriding some of the inherited methods. In the {{ll|JavaDocs}}, subclasses are listed in the "Direct Known Subclasses" section of the class page. The hierarchy tree with parents is shown at the top of the class page and its inherited methods and fields are listed in the "Method Summary" and "Field Summary" sections of the class page. {{Clear}} === Nested classes === A subclass inherits another class, while a '''nested class''' is defined directly in a class and as such has access to even private methods and fields from its original class. In the {{ll|JavaDocs}}, nested classes are listed in the “Nested Class Summary” section of the class page. Nested classes are written as ClassName.NestedClassName. {{Note|This principle is not too important to understand to work with the Lua API and mostly a technical detail, however there are some notable nested classes which are often used, such as the [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/characters/skills/PerkFactory.Perks.html PerkFactory.Perks] for example.}} === Instance and static === Java classes can have two types of methods and fields: instance methods and static methods. To run, instance methods require an instance of the class, while static methods can be run without an instance. === Access Modifiers === Java class members have an access modifier (public, protected, package, private) which determines where they are accessible. Only public members are exposed to Lua. === Methods and fields === Java classes can have methods and fields which are respectively functions and variables associated to the class if private or unique to an instance of the class. == Exposed elements == Not all the Java classes and methods are exposed to the Lua API. In the {{ll|JavaDocs}}, there is no indication of which classes are exposed but for the classes that are exposed, it shows only the methods that are exposed. To call a static method, you need to use the syntax {{Code|ClassName.methodName(args...)|lang=lua}} , while for instance methods, you need to use the syntax {{Code|instance:methodName(args...)|lang=lua}} . This directly refers to the Lua syntax for calling {{ll|Lua objects}} methods with the colon {{Code|:|lang=lua}} operator passing {{Code|self|lang=lua}} (the instance here) as the first argument, while the dot {{Code|.|lang=lua}} operator is used for static methods. For example [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/characters/IsoPlayer.html#getLocalPlayerByOnlineID(short) {{Code|getLocalPlayerByOnlineID(ID)|lang=lua}}] can be ran without an instance of IsoPlayer ({{Code|IsoPlayer.getLocalPlayerByOnlineID(ID)|lang=lua}} ), while [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/characters/IsoPlayer.html#getForname() {{Code|getForname()}}] needs an instance of IsoPlayer to be ran ({{Code|player:getForname()|lang=lua}} ). [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/Lua/LuaManager.GlobalObject.html LuaManager.GlobalObject] defines global methods which are exposed in peculiar way, not following the usual way to use them described above. Static methods listed in the JavaDocs page for LuaManager.GlobalObject are called simply by like global Lua functions, such as [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/Lua/LuaManager.GlobalObject.html#getCell() {{Code|getPlayer()|lang=lua}}] or [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/Lua/LuaManager.GlobalObject.html#getPlayer() {{Code|getCell()|lang=lua}}] . {{Note|Class objects from the Java are not the same as {{ll|Lua objects}}! They are not tables, but rather direct links to the Java classes. As such, they cannot be used as Lua objects and do not have the same properties as Lua objects.}} === Accessing fields === === Static fields === Public static fields of exposed classes are exposed to Lua in a global table of the same name as the class. {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local DEATH_MUSIC_NAME = IsoPlayer.DEATH_MUSIC_NAME }} === Instance fields === {{Note|type=error|Accessing fields is no longer possible since {{ll|Build 42.15.0}} due to reflection being restricted to {{ll|debug mode}} only for security reasons. Static fields can still be accessed without any problems however.}} Instance fields are different as they are not directly exposed but can be accessed by using reflection. It involves a fairly complex set of operations: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local function getJavaField(object, field) -- (IsoZombie instance, "strength") local offset = string.len(field) for i = 0, getNumClassFields(object) - 1 do local m = getClassField(object, i) if string.sub(tostring(m), -offset) == field then return getClassFieldVal(object, m) end end return nil -- no field found end }} This can access any field declared by the class, regardless of whether it is private or public. {{Note|type=warn|Accessing the inherited fields of a class from one of its subclass is not possible currently.}} === Constructor === Constructors are used to instantiate a Java class. This is done with the following way: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = ClassName.new(args...) }} The ClassName of course needs to be the name of the Java class, so for example IsoZombie, while the arguments args are specific to the Java class. If you want to instantiate an IsoZombie, you can use its associated [https://projectzomboid.com/modding/zombie/characters/IsoZombie.html#(zombie.iso.IsoCell) constructor] . {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- create the IsoZombie instance local isoZombie = IsoZombie.new(getCell()) }} Something very important to take note of is that this will not create an actual zombie, but simply an instance of IsoZombie which can be used for different operations which require an IsoZombie instance. This is the usual usage of the constructor, and creating entities is mostly done with different kinds of methods. This IsoZombie instance can be used to create a corpse, for example with the following method for {{ll|Build 41}}: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- square is an IsoGridSquare square:addCorpse(IsoDeadBody.new(zombie), false) -- note the use of IsoDeadBody constructor here }} === Example === {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = --- INSTANCE METHOD EXAMPLE --- -- retrieve the client IsoPlayer instance local player = getPlayer() -- a LuaManager.GlobalObject method -- retrieve the IsoPlayer instance move speed local moveSpeed = player:getMoveSpeed() -- instance method, notice the ":" --- STATIC METHOD EXAMPLE --- -- retrieve the list of IsoPlayers local players = IsoPlayer.getPlayers() -- static method, notice the "." }} === Hooking to Java methods === It is possible to hook to Java methods, which means to run Lua code when a specific Java method **is called Lua side**. This has the disadvantage that your hook will not be called if the method is called Java side, but it can have niche uses in some cases: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local index = __classmetatables[ClassName.class].__index local old_method = index.method function index:method(...) old_method(self, ...) end }} {{Note|type=warn|You cannot hook to Java methods which are called Java side!}} == Lua objects == Lua objects are widely used in the Lua API and natively defined in it. They utilize the {{ll|ISBaseObject}} class and {{ll|derive}} from it to define new classes which can themselves be derived from. They are usually global and can be accessed from anywhere but in some cases where they are locked behind a local scope to a file, you can utilize the {{ll|DOME}} library to access them. {{ll|Timed Actions}} use Lua objects to easily instantiate them and derive directly from {{ll|ISBaseTimedAction}}. UI elements also use Lua objects. == Where to start == To setup a programming environment, see the {{ll|Getting started#Programming environment|getting started}} page. Programming with the Lua (API) can be done in many ways, but in most cases it will involve using a {{ll|Lua event}} to run your code at specific moments of the game. As such, it's suggested to check out the [[:Category:Lua events|events]] which are available to see where you can get started. When this didn't do much for you, another thing you might be interested to is to either check the vanilla code or for a mod which does something similar and see how they achieve it. With experience, you can learn to understand the game code and create your own functionalities more easily without needing to use examples. Alternatively, various guides available on the Wiki will explain how to do certain actions. === Community libraries ===

=== Community libraries === There are various community libraries which can help you with your Lua modding. For a full list, see the {{ll|Modding projects}} in the [[:Category:Libraries|libraries category]] . == Folder structure == {{Main|Mod structure}} '''Lua''' scripts, with the file extension .lua need to be inside three subfolders inside the media/lua folder, and are used to determine the loading of files in singleplayer and multiplayer: {{CodeSnip | code = 📁 media 📁 lua 📁 client 📄 yourFile.lua ... 📁 server 📄 yourOtherFile.lua ... 📁 shared 📄 thisIsALuaScript.lua ... }} The only time one of these folder is not loaded is for multiplayer server side: {| class="wikitable theme-blue" |+ style="white-space:nowrap" | Which folders are loaded in which game mode ! Folder !! Singleplayer !! Multiplayer:
client side !! Multiplayer:
server side |- | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| client | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Cross.png]] |- | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| server | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] |- | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| shared | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] | style="min-width: 100px;text-align: center;"| [[File:UI Tick.png]] |} Organization inside the client, server and shared folders is free and subfolders can be created with files named in any way. Files with the same relative path to the lua as vanilla files will overwrite them, so make sure to use unique names and relative paths. This applies to other mod files too and is impacted by the load order between mods. {{Note|A good trick to not have your Lua files clash with other mods or vanilla files is to put your Lua files inside subfolders named after your mod. This will make it unlikely for your mod to clash with other mods.}} === Load order === Lua files are loaded when launching the game, and when exiting a save, or when manually triggered in {{ll|debug mode}} in the main menu, in the following order: # Shared - vanilla files # Shared - mod files # Client - vanilla files # Client - mod files The server subfolder is actually loaded only when launching a save, so anytime Lua is loaded or reloaded the server files are unloaded until a save is loaded. The order for the server subfolder files is:
  1. Server - vanilla files
  2. Server - mod files
{{Note|Translation files are also put inside the lua folder but are not Lua files. See the {{ll|Translations}} page for more detail.}} {{Note|type=warn|It is not recommended to overwrite existing files if not needed for compatibility reasons. Instead, overwrite specific functions or {{ll|Lua (language)#Decoration|hook}} them when possible.}} == See also == * {{ll|Java}} - explains things related to * {{ll|Lua (language)}} - the programming language used in Project Zomboid. * {{ll|Lua objects}} - classes defined in the Lua. * {{ll|Lua event}} - events which can be used to run Lua code at specific moments of the game. * {{ll|LuaDocs}} - an unofficial project which acts like a JavaDocs but for the Lua API. * {{ll|ModOptions}} - the native mod options API introduced in {{ll|Build 42}}. * {{ll|User Interface}} - explains how to make a UI via the Lua API. == Navigation == {{Navbox modding}} {{ll|Category:Modding}} {{ll|Category:Modding guides}} ==== {{Navbar modding}} {{Page version|42.13.1}} '''Networking''' is a process needed to handle client/server interactions, allowing for the exchange of data and commands between the two to properly sync. This guide will not explain when networking should be used, but rather how to implement it. Since {{ll|Build 42.13.1}} release, server side handles most of the logic for player damage, item stats etc. This means you need to set any of these from the server side instead of the client side and then use sync functions to sync specifically what you changed. == Client/Server only code == When writing code that should only run on the client or server, you can use the following checks: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = if isClient() then -- this code is ran client side elseif isServer() then -- this code is ran server side else -- this code is ran in singleplayer end }} You can user a helper function to check if the code is ran in singleplayer: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local function isSinglePlayer() return not isClient() and not isServer() end }} These methods can be used to have client/server or singleplayer only specific Lua files by adding at the very top of your lua files the following which will skip the entire file content based on the environment it is ran in: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- most commonly used: file should load only on the server side or in singleplayer if isClient() then return end }} {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- file should load only on the client side or in singleplayer -- you can also accomplish this by placing your file in the lua/client/ directory if isServer() then return end }} {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- file should load only on the client side and not in singleplayer if not isClient() then return end }} {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- file should load only on the server side and not in singleplayer if not isServer() then return end }} {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- file should load only in singleplayer if isClient() or isServer() then return end }} Use these to skip loading functions or variables in an environment that does not need them. === Client status === To check if the client is an admin, you can use {{Code|lang=lua|isAdmin()}} from client side, and from server side you can use {{Code|lang=Java|IsoPlayer.getAccessLevel()}} : {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = -- if ran client side, check if the client is an admin -- else, check if it's singleplayer, meaning the player has admin rights -- use this based on what your mod needs to do for both situations local function checkClientIsAdmin() return isClient() and isAdmin() or isSinglePlayer() end }} == Commands == The main method used for networking is the ''command'' system. Commands are sent from one side (client or server) to the other, and are handled by a function on the receiving side. Commands can be sent with or without parameters, and can be sent to all clients, a specific client, or the server and intercepted by the use of specific {{ll|Lua event}}s. Commands can be identified with the use a {{Code|lang=lua|module}} , which is suggested to be your mod name, and {{Code|lang=lua|command}} name. The transmitted data can only hold plain old data (strings, booleans, numbers, and tables), so no {{ll|Java object}} instances such as the player ({{JavaObject|IsoPlayer|package=zombie/characters}} ) or an inventory ({{JavaObject|InventoryContainer|package=zombie/inventory/types}} ). [[File:Networking.png|center|800px|class=logo-dark]] === Client to server === The client sends commands to the server with the use of the following: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua | code = local args = {} -- put any data inside this table sendClientCommand("ModuleName", "CommandName", args) }} And the server intercepts the client commands with the use of {{ll|OnClientCommand}}: {{CodeSnip | lang = lua

For teleportation, I'm noting that player:teleportTo exists on IsoGameCharacter but need to consider multiplayer anticheat implications in 42.21.

Since client-side teleports could trigger anti-cheat flags, I'm deciding to keep blink as single-player-only functionality, falling back to an endurance boost in multiplayer via isClient() checks, rather than risking a flagged teleport. Flight and speed effects fall back to endurance refill when setRunSpeedModifier is unavailable, and the auto-sort inventory feature can safely use the vanilla ISInventoryTransferAction since it's already MP-safe.

For zombie health changes, I'm recognizing that client-side setHealth calls aren't authoritative in multiplayer — the server needs to handle this, so I'm working out how the client should pass the zombie's online ID along with coordinates so the server can locate and search for the correct zombie in its list.

I'm now designing a unified server-side "Fx router" command that validates the effect key, checks distance and cooldown constraints, pulls power costs from server sandbox settings rather than trusting the client, and resolves targets (self, world, or foe) by matching online IDs or finding the nearest zombie, with single-player fallback since online IDs may not resolve there. This means restructuring the effect definitions so they live server-side while clients only detect triggers and request effects by key and target.

I'm marking each effect as client-only or server-handled -- visual-local things like the neon halo and auto timed actions stay client-side, while everything else routes through the server. In server contexts like NPC guard or creature mechanics, I'll just skip the client-only effects rather than trying to sync them back down.

For singleplayer, sendClientCommand calls the handler directly per the official doc, so that path is fine. The trickier case is server-side body damage changes syncing to the client, and zombie-target abilities where the effect actually targets the player (the zombie's target) rather than the zombie itself -- I need the server to resolve the correct player id there.

I'm defining a client helper requestFx(player, key, target) that defaults target to the player itself, builds position args, and flags whether the target is the player ("self") or a zombie (by online id), then sends it via sendClientCommand. On the server side I'm starting the Commands.fx handler that validates config and args before processing.

Writing server fx handler...

For the fallback when no Cooldown config exists, I'll default the server-side rate limit to a fraction of the configured cooldown, falling back to 250ms for mechanics that are purely server-driven.

Thinking through item area releases, I realize rate-limiting by key would wrongly drop repeated foe-hit calls within one radius release. Better to restructure so the client just sends a single release command and the server handles the radius scan, falloff, and application entirely — client does detection and UI, server owns all game-state logic.

For weapon procs, I'm thinking client-side `OnHitZombie` checks if the attacker is the local player, then sends a proc command with position data; the server verifies the weapon is actually equipped, rolls cooldown/chance, and applies bonus damage and effects itself. For item/magic release, since timed actions' `complete()` always runs server-side (even in singleplayer), that's the right place to put the release logic — it lives in the shared timed action file, with effects code guarded appropriately since it's shared.

This leads me toward a clean file structure: a shared Config file, a shared Effects module holding all server-authoritative foe/self/world effects plus target-finding and area helpers, a shared Actions file for timed actions, a client file for triggers/UI/requests, and a server file for the command router, loot, and timers. Client-only cosmetic effects like neon/auto visuals stay isolated in the client file. I'm also noting that a "lite" mode variant inlines its config directly rather than referencing the shared config.

 Modding Policy 
 Last Updated: 04/10/2022 
 Hello survivor! Here’s the scoop on modding Project Zomboid. By mods, we mean modifications of Project Zomboid (or part of it) and/or new content or tools made for it by you, whether standalone or integrated. Long story short, you can make mods, but must follow the rules below. 
 This Modding Policy should be read alongside the Project Zomboid Terms and Conditions (which are legally binding on you), Valve’s Mod Content Usage Policy , and Valve’s Steam Subscriber Agreement . We may update this Modding Policy from time to time – so we recommend you check it periodically. 
 1. Your responsibility 
 1.1. Modders are solely responsible for: 
 1.1.1. their mod, including (but not limited to compliance with any hosting platforms such as Steam Workshop). 
 1.1.2. obtaining the necessary consents or licences for any third-party materials in the mod. (This includes if you want to use assets or materials from another mod – you need their permission to use it yourself). 
 1.2. Users of mods are responsible for their usage of mods – we don’t check them, and we can’t be responsible for them. 
 2. Modding restrictions 
 2.1. If you are a player that uses mods: respect the time, dedication and talent of your favourite modders. Remember that they have lives too and are generally not remunerated for their time or skills. They will update their mods as soon as they can and haranguing them will not speed up the process. 
 2.2. Mod content. You are allowed to edit Project Zomboid in any way you want, provided that you do not: 
 2.2.1. edit it in such a way that it is either intentionally damaging to people’s PCs or other devices, removes the login system, or enables people to play Project Zomboid (or parts of it) without purchasing. This clearly also covers all future unreleased content and versions of Project Zomboid. 
 2.2.2. create nor publish content that is objectionable and inappropriate. This includes but is not limited to content that is intentionally offensive, abusive, obscene, discriminatory, racist, pornographic, aimed to harass someone or a group of people, threatening, hateful, xenophobic, invasive to the privacy of another person or group of people, sexist, and/or defamatory. 
 2.2.3. call or make your mod appear to be “Official”. 
 2.3. Donations. Modders are free to receive monetary/gift donations from the players who use their releases, and appreciate the time and effort put into them. However, having mods created exclusively for those who choose to donate (or separate ‘in-mod’ content and bonuses) is not allowed. 
 2.4. Commercialisation. Unless any arrangements to the contrary have been made with us, mod creators cannot sell access to a mod and/or mod content. Mod creators are permitted to work on commissioned mods provided such mods are not sold. Please see section 4 of the Terms & Conditions for more information on this. 
 2.5. Political Statements. We reserve the right to remove content that displays any overt political messaging (from any side of any argument, and from any nation) that we reasonably believe could cause disruption within our community or more broadly. 
 Whether The Indie Stone, or most, would agree with the statements made is not relevant – as it’s a dangerous precedent that modders can add political messaging of any kind that could silently update in the background without it being evident that messaging wasn’t made directly by the developers. 
 (If you don’t like a mod author’s choice to add anything you do not appreciate to their mod, unsubscribe, perhaps leave a polite comment if that is your wish, and move on. Harassment will not be tolerated.) 
 2.6. Hidden / Unexpected Content. Any hidden or unexpected content and/or messages made in updates to mods that are not flagged on the Steam Workshop description / pages or isn’t evident in the mod itself must have attribution VISIBLE as to where (and from whom) said content has originated. 
 2.7. Be Lovely. Following this mantra, we ask mod authors to be respectful to other players, other modders and the time everyone has put into supporting Project Zomboid. Do not say anything that is unlawful, gives rise to civil or criminal liability or could harm the game, its players, or The Indie Stone. 
 3. Ownership 
 3.1. You own mods that you create. We own Project Zomboid, our other property and everything in them. 
 3.2. We need a right to use your mods so that we can distribute them, and so that others can play them through Project Zomboid. In legal terms, you grant us a non-exclusive, permanent, sub-licensable, royalty-free, irrevocable, and worldwide licence to use, modify, reproduce, create derivative works from, distribute, transmit, perform communicate and exploit your mods (or any part of them) in connection with Project Zomboid. 
 In all circumstances Spiffo’s Workshop abides by the exact same rules as Valve for mods made for Project Zomboid and hosted on the Steam Workshop. 
 “It’s a sad fact, but in some cases content is [also being] lifted from one mod to another. It’s often a misconception that just because a mod is free to download, its contents are also free for you to take and choose from as you wish.” 
 “Even if a mod is free or not, the creators of any original work included within it (sounds, materials, models, source code) own the copyright for their work. This is true if you are a high-school kid, a corporation, or just some other modder who puts stuff together for fun. Every author gains these rights by default when they create their work.”

If you see something in another mod that would be of use to you in your own mod or map, your first step should be to contact the mod team and then specifically ask the creator of the item you’re after. They and they alone can give you permission to use their work.”

 4.1. Modification of other users’ workshop submissions is allowed under personal use, but you are NOT allowed to submit work that is not your own, without permission of the mod owner.

 4.3. Even if permission not to credit a mod owner is obtained, if a mod creator raises an issue with our moderation staff, failing to credit modders for any substantially unique or direct link to their work will potentially result in your own mod being delisted until credit is given. 
 5. Our use of your mods 
 5.1. We are, technically, permitted under Steam’s Subscriber Agreement to incorporate any mods submitted to Steam into Project Zomboid. 
 5.2. However, as a matter of policy, should this ever happen with Project Zomboid (and the relatively infrequent occasions when it has happened in the past) it is after direct communication and signed agreement between all parties. Upon allowing The Indie Stone to use a modification in the game modders cannot claim entitlement to any past, current or future profits from the game unless this is agreed upon at the time.

While we will respect people’s personal creations and always ask for permission and offer credit within the game before intentionally including any code, art or dialogue directly from mods with the core game: we do this out of respect to the authors and are not legally obliged.

 7.1.2. Semi-Private. These are packs that are usually tailored to a customised server experience, and are posted as “Unlisted” on the Steam Workshop. These modpacks still require permission. Mod authors who find their mods in an Unlisted modpack are still free to ask to have their mod pulled, or for the modpack to be removed from the Workshop until their mod has been taken out.

It is essential for {{ll|Uploading mods|publishing a mod}} and ensuring that it can be found and downloaded by other players ({{ll|mods}}) or servers ({{ll|SteamCMD}}). To find this ID, you can: * Check the URL of your mod on the Steam Workshop. The ID is the number at the end of the URL. * Find it at the bottom of the mod's page if it was uploaded from the {{ll|Uploading mods#In-game uploader|in-game uploader}}. == See also == * {{ll|App ID}} – the unique identifier for a game or application on the Steam platform. * {{ll|Game files}} – the files and assets that make up a game. == Navigation == {{Navbox modding}} {{ll|Category:Modding}} {{Navbar modding}} {{Page version|42.20.2}} This page will explain the process of '''uploading mods''' to the Steam Workshop with the in-game uploader, as well as documenting alternative methods and uploaders that give more control over what you do. {{Note|type=warn|When uploading a mod with files deleted from the previous version, users will not have these files removed automatically and might get version mismatch errors. You can simply leave the files in but replace the content to leave them empty.}} == In-game uploader == The in-game uploader can be accessed from the main menu in the Workshop menu, then ''"Create and update items"''. This menu will show every valid mod in your {{ll|Mod structure#Workshop folder|Workshop folder}} and allow you to upload them to the Steam Workshop. After selecting which mod to upload/update, you will be prompted with a menu to set the mod's title, description, tags, and visibility. The preview image is also visible here. If you want to keep the description of your mod, you will need to copy it before uploading! A solution to this problem is anytime you update your mod, copy the description from the Steam Workshop page and paste it in the uploader's description field. Make sure to remove the workshop and mod ID at the end of the copied description, or you will end up uploading duplicates of it.}} {{Note|type=warn|You can find a description of the result codes in the [https://partner.steamgames.com/doc/api/steam_api#EResult Steamworks SDK API reference]. These are rarely too descriptive of the actual problem but they can help you find out what could be wrong.}} == Alternative uploaders == * {{ll|SteamCMD#Uploading Workshop items|SteamCMD}} – the official {{ll|Steam}} command line tool that allows you to upload mods with a build configuration file. This method is more complex but allows for more control over the upload process and its content. * [https://github.com/TechnologicNick/SteamChangePreview SteamChangePreview tool] – allows you to bypass the limitations of the in-game uploader to be able to upload different-sized preview images for your mod on its Steam page. It notably allows you to upload a non-square image, a higher resolution image, or an animated preview image. * {{ll|Steam Uploader}} – an external uploader that provides the ability to update different elements on a Workshop page independently or multiple ones together (description, preview, content…). == Navigation == {{Navbox modding}} {{ll|Category:Modding guides}}

I'm noting that on Nxeon PZ servers, the config cache directory maps to the host path, so a local mod would need to be installed at the mods folder under that config directory, with the server path being relative to the Zomboid mods folder.

The bigger issue is that clients need identical files — if a mod isn't on Steam Workshop, players have to manually copy it into their own Zomboid/mods folder for checksums to match. Publishing to Workshop requires the mod creator's own Steam account with the game owned, since uploading via SteamCMD's workshop_build_item needs a logged-in account that owns the game — Cyrus can't do this on their behalf, so this is a decision point for the key owner to flag.

I'm also confirming that the dedicated server loads mods from both the local Zomboid/mods folder and the Workshop folder, though I should mark this as needing an end-to-end test to be sure. For the rest of the spell effects, I'm sketching out server-side logic for each: thunder events for storms, SP-only teleport for blink with an endurance substitute in multiplayer, server-side health restoration for heal, poison applied to player stats or zombie damage, and zombie summoning using the outfit and pathfinding sound functions.

Since Zomboid has no real flight, I'm reusing the shared "flight" effect label but treating it in-game as an endurance/fatigue refill, noting the label mismatch is minor since the feature labels come from a shared kit file I can't easily override per-game. For the remaining effects, I'm planning panic status or target-clearing for void, night-only fatigue/damage for lunar, and continuing to outline the auto effect.

For auto and neon, these are client-only effects—auto queues an inventory transfer action locally, neon just adds a visual halo note—so they fire immediately on the client rather than through server validation. Server-authoritative effects (weapon procs, zombie abilities, vehicle rams) instead go through a command request or execute directly in server-side completion/timers.

I'm now tracing where triggers originate: on the client, hitting a zombie checks if the attacker is local and wielding the right weapon, does a cooldown precheck, then requests the effect; the server independently re-verifies the weapon, rolls cooldown/chance, scales bonus damage by condition, and applies effects to the target zombie located via online ID—falling back to nearest zombie search in singleplayer where online ID isn't meaningful.

For items/magic, effects release server-side when a timed action completes, with purely client-only effects applied during the perform phase. For creature abilities, the client detects zombie variants and requests an ability using the zombie's online ID, while the server independently confirms the zombie exists, is actually a variant, and is within radius, enforcing per-zombie cooldowns and periodic pack drops on death. I'm also considering that setting walk type or health on variant zombies client-side could desync in multiplayer since zombie movement is server/owner-simulated, so that logic should move server-side at spawn time, while variant detection on the client relies on a deterministic roll based on the zombie's persistent outfit ID rather than synced mod data.

Since OnZombieUpdate doesn't fire server-side, I'll have the server set walk type only for zombies it spawns in packs, leaving client-spawned natural variants with correct abilities but vanilla speed — a reasonable tradeoff. NPC trading flows through a shared timed action where the server verifies money, removes bills, and adds goods with price computed server-side. For vehicles, client-side engine boost via keybind likely works since the driver's client simulates vehicle physics, but I'm unsure about sync behavior for setEngineFeature, so I'll keep that client-side while routing ram effects through a server request.

For "ram," I'll have the client send position data and let the server apply effects to zombies within range, validating the player is actually in a vehicle moving above a speed threshold using getVehicle() and getCurrentSpeedKmHour(). World anomaly effects should move server-side entirely — applied directly to the player in the server handler rather than client-side, with the client only rendering the visual halo. ADVANCED-MODS.md
RENDERS-AND-TEXTURES.md
- Every other game moved under modders' feet in the last 90 days: Palworld 1.0 (2026-07-10), Terraria 1.4.5 (2026-01-27 [S]) which tModLoader does not yet ship for, Valheim 1.0 (2026-09-09, "piece categories overhauled", Jotunn rewritten for 1.0.7), Project Zomboid Build 42.20 stable (2026-07-29), Rust's monthly Thursday update. Training data for these games is mostly pre-change.
- Published evidence agrees: version-controllable code generation is "a significant challenge, even for GPT-4o" ([VersiCode](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07411)); valid calls to low-frequency APIs were 38.6% for GPT-4o, rising to 47.9% with documentation retrieval, and badly chosen retrieval cut high-frequency accuracy by 39 points ([CloudAPIBench / DAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09726)); and compile-pass rate can be anti-correlated with functional correctness ([Mage](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.07342)).

**Honest AI assessment by game (today).**

| Game | Best-supported "advanced" targets | Needs a human |
|---|---|---|
| Minecraft Paper/Purpur | Commands, GUIs, economies, quests, minigames, admin tooling, custom items via data components (R1 to R2) | World-gen tuning, balance, custom blocks, resource-pack art, Folia-safe rewrites (R3) |
| Terraria tModLoader | Items, buffs, recipes, simple NPCs and projectiles (R1 to R2) | Bosses, tiles, world gen, netcode edge cases, IL patching (R3) |
| Terraria TShock | Server commands, permissions, anti-grief, events (R1 to R2) | Anything needing new items or art (impossible server-only) |
| Valheim (BepInEx + Jotunn) | Config and stat changes, clone-and-modify items, recipes, status effects (R1 to R2) | New models and prefabs (Unity editor), new biomes (R3) |
| Rust (Oxide/Carbon) | Kits, teleports, shops, custom UI, anti-cheat tooling (R1 to R2) | New items or models (impossible server-side), monthly-update triage (needs monitoring) |
| Palworld | PalSchema JSON data mods (R2) | UE4SS Lua without an SDK dump, Blueprint LogicMods, cooked assets (R3) |
| Project Zomboid | Item/recipe scripts and small Lua (R2, once B42 golden examples exist) | Models, maps, anything mixing B41 knowledge (R3) |

**Three hard platform facts Cyrus should surface to customers**
1. **Palworld server-side mods are Windows-server only** per community docs quoting the official docs [S: [XGamingServer](https://xgamingserver.com/docs/palworld/mod-installation), [ConnectHosting](https://connecthosting.net/blog/palworld-server-mods-what-works), [gamever.io](https://gamever.io/knowledge-base/server-side-mods-in-palworld-palmodsettingsini-and-the-flag-that-undoes-everything)]. Nxeon's Palworld image is the native Linux server (config path `.../Config/LinuxServer/PalWorldSettings.ini`) [L: `lib/game-control.ts:239`]. Unless that is wrong, most Palworld mods cannot run on Nxeon's Palworld servers today. This must be checked before the Palworld agent's `side` and `reason` strings are written.
2. **tModLoader and TShock cannot be combined**: tModLoader stable (v2026.08.3.0) targets Terraria 1.4.4; TShock 6.2.1 targets Terraria 1.4.5.8 [V: GitHub release APIs]. tModLoader has an active `1.4.5` branch (last commit 2026-10-07) [V], so this will change; Cyrus's version table must treat them as two products.
3. **Rust and Palworld-style "new item" ideas cannot be delivered server-side.** Vanilla Rust clients only show existing prefabs and Facepunch-approved workshop skins [S]. Cyrus should refuse or reframe those requests honestly.

**What Cyrus should add (ranked; details in section 9).**
1. Per-game **version-and-API knowledge packs** generated from the real jars, SDKs and docs, injected only for the target version (the Minecraft "sheets plus failure rules" pattern, generalised). Highest value, medium effort per game.
2. A **structured spec card** (commands, permissions, configs, GUIs, acceptance tests) before code, shared by all games. It also feeds tests.
3. **Golden examples** per game, human-verified and compile-tested, retrieved by nearest match. These double as regression tests.
4. **Multi-file projects with typed file roles** (code, config, data, lang, assets) and diff-based edits.
5. A **verification ladder** per game (static lint, compile, unit tests of pure logic, live smoke test on a throwaway server where the game allows).
6. **Dependency handling** (declared soft-dependencies, compile-only API digests, install-time "requires X" warnings).
7. **Iterative refinement from real server logs**, then multi-step planning for large mods, then companion asset packs (see `RENDERS-AND-TEXTURES.md`).

# Project Zomboid: API check for the Cyrus generator (2026-10-08)

Every Java method the generator emits was checked against the **42.21 JavaDocs** (albion.codeberg.page/PZ-JavaDocs, "PZ API Documentation 42.21.0"), every vanilla Lua function against the **42.20.3 LuaDocs** (demiurgequantified.github.io/ProjectZomboidLuaDocs) and the **Umbrella** typings (github.com/PZ-Umbrella/Umbrella, last commit 2026-09-28), and every script/translation format against **The Indie Stone's own migration guides** for 42.13 and 42.15 and the **PZ API Docs** script reference (generated from 42.21). The old handoff generator had no `plausible:` tags, but it was written against early Build 42 and several of its calls no longer exist.

Note on sources: early in this session I fetched a few pzwiki.net pages as raw wikitext with `curl` (WebFetch got a 403). The coordinator then said pzwiki is behind Cloudflare and must not be bypassed. I stopped, and every fact in the shipped files is now sourced from the primary sources above; pzwiki is not cited anywhere.

## Removed or wrong in the old generator (fixed)

| Old call / format | Status in 42.21 | Replacement |
|---|---|---|
| `getStats():getFatigue()/setFatigue()`, `getEndurance/setEndurance`, `getPanic/setPanic` | Gone (Stats has only `get/set/add(CharacterStat, …)`) | `getStats():add(CharacterStat.X, delta)` via a guarded `nudge()` helper |
| `getBodyDamage():getPoisonLevel()/setPoisonLevel()`, `getTemperature()/setTemperature()` | Gone from BodyDamage | `CharacterStat.POISON`, `CharacterStat.TEMPERATURE` |
| `IsoPlayer:setRunSpeedModifier()` | Does not exist | "second wind": endurance up, fatigue down |
| `getMoodles():getNumMoodles()` | Does not exist | HUD shows `CharacterStat.STRESS` |
| `who:setLx()/setLy()` | Do not exist (`setLastX/setLastY`) | `character:teleportTo(x, y, z)`; on a dedicated server the blink becomes a stamina burst (no client teleports) |
| `square:Is(IsoFlagType.water)` | `Is` gone; `has(IsoFlagType)` / `isWaterSquare()` | `square:isWaterSquare()` |
| `OnWeaponHitCharacter` for zombie hits | Sources disagree on whether zombies fire it | `OnHitZombie(zombie, attacker, bodyPart, weapon)` |
| Item `Type = Weapon`, `DisplayName = …` | Removed in 42.13 | `ItemType = base:weapon`, name in `ItemName.json` |
| Weapon `Categories = Axe/Blunt` | Registry ids since 42.13 | `base:axe` / `base:blunt` (WeaponCategory fields AXE, BLUNT…) |
| Recipe `tags[Screwdriver]` | Registry ids since 42.13 | `tags[base:screwdriver]` (ItemTag doc lists it) |
| `IG_UI_EN.txt`, `Sandbox_EN.txt` Lua tables | Not loaded since 42.15 | `IG_UI.json`, `Sandbox.json` (+ `ItemName.json`, `Recipes.json`, `Mod.json`) |
| Timed actions in `lua/client`, items changed client side | Broken in 42.13+ MP | `lua/shared/<Mod>/Actions.lua`, `getDuration()`, `complete()` with `UseAndSync`, `syncItemFields`, `instanceItem` + `sendAddItemToContainer` / `sendRemoveItemFromContainer` |
| Quest reward `player:getXp():AddXP`, `AddItem` on the client | Anti-cheat / deleted on relog | server command → `addXp(player, Perks.X, n)` + server-side item |
| Trade action `new(character, npc, cost)` | Field names must equal arg names; price must not come from the client | `new(character)`, price computed in `complete()` |
| `sendServerCommand` to drive client UI in singleplayer | OnServerCommand is multiplayer-only; sendServerCommand does nothing on a client | `notify()` helper: `sendServerCommand` on a server, `triggerEvent("OnServerCommand", …)` otherwise |
| `42/media/maps/<Mod>/spawnpoints.lua` + `map.info` with `lots=Muldraugh, KY` | Untested half-map; risks a broken map entry | dropped; the world archetype is Lua-only (zone + loot + anomalies) |
| `getWorld():registerZone(...)` on map load | Exists, but adds an unknown zone type for no gameplay value | dropped |
| `module Base` for items | Clashes with vanilla ids | own module (`module <ModId> { imports { Base } }`) |
| mod.info `poster=poster.png`, `icon=icon.png` with no files | Mod manager shows no image | omitted until art exists; listed in ASSETS.md |

Events (Umbrella): OnHitZombie, OnZombieUpdate (client), OnPlayerUpdate (client), OnExitVehicle (client), OnZombieDead, OnPreDistributionMerge, OnFillInventoryObjectContextMenu, OnFillWorldObjectContextMenu, OnClientCommand (server), OnServerCommand (MP client), OnReceiveGlobalModData (MP), EveryHours, EveryTenMinutes, EveryOneMinute.

## Still unverified (also in the GameSupport `unknowns`)

- `CharacterStat` reachable as a Lua global (guarded with `if CharacterStat`).
- Server-side stat/health changes reaching the client screen immediately in MP.
- Server-side `setWalkType` mirrored to clients.

- Vanilla crafting category names other than the documented default `Miscellaneous`.

# Project Zomboid in Cyrus: readiness checklist and explainer (2026-10-08)

Status: **not live** (`soon`). Flipping it to live is the owner's decision. Branch `feature/cyrus-v6-game-zomboid`.

## What is done

- `lib/cyrus/games/zomboid.ts`: verified GameSupport (versions 42.21 → 41.78, install side `both`, plain-language install text, 17 dangerous-API rules, breakage risks with guards, outdated signals, categories, sources, unknowns) plus a `knowledge` pack (14 API-sheet lines, 12 Build 41→42 failure rules with regex detectors).
- `lib/cyrus/engine/games/zomboid.ts`: the template generator rewritten for Build 42.15+ and the 42.13 multiplayer rules (server-authoritative effects, shared timed actions, JSON translations, `ItemType`/registry ids, own script module, per-mod Lua folders, guarded fire, no map files). API check: `API-CHECK.md`.
- `lib/cyrus/games/zomboid.validate.ts`: static validator (layout, mod.info, Lua 5.1 structure lint written in TypeScript, dangerous APIs, failure rules, MP rules, script braces, JSON translations).
- `test/cyrus-game-zomboid.test.ts`: every category × model × six prompts must pass the validator with zero blocking issues, plus negative tests.

## What is left before it can go live

1. **Real-model generation path.** Today Zomboid output comes from the deterministic template, not from the AI build service (which only builds Minecraft). The live product needs the build service to: take the GameSupport `knowledge` pack as context, generate, run `validateZomboidMod`, feed blocking issues back for repair, and only then show the mod. Owner decision: when to wire it, and whether Zomboid gets its own service endpoint.
2. **Load test in a sandbox (not run).** Needs nothing proprietary in git, but it needs compute:
   - Project Zomboid dedicated server, downloaded by SteamCMD anonymously (app **380870**) inside a throwaway container, the same way Nxeon's own Zomboid image installs it. Nothing is redistributed: Valve's tool fetches it into the sandbox.
   - Steps: copy the mod into `<cachedir>/mods/<ModId>/`, set `Mods=<ModId>` in `Server/servertest.ini`, boot with a fresh world, wait for "SERVER STARTED", run a few game minutes, then grep `console.txt` / `Logs/*DebugLog-server.txt` for `ERROR`, `STACK TRACE`, `attempted index`, `Object tried to call nil` mentioning the mod's files. Exit code + log excerpt = the verdict.
   - Lua unit tests: run the generated busted spec with a free Lua 5.1 (`lua5.1` + `busted`, or the open-source `wasmoon`/`fengari` npm packages). Not installed anywhere today; adding them is a dependency or system-package decision for the owner.
   - Limits: a headless server never runs `lua/client` code, so HUDs, context menus and keybinds still need a human (or a scripted client, which is not available).
   - Resources: about 4 to 6 GB RAM and 2 vCPU per test run (Build 42 is heavy; Nxeon sells 6 GB as the smallest Zomboid plan). Must run on a sandbox VM, never on the build VM or a customer VM.
3. **End-to-end test on a real Nxeon 42.21 server.** Confirm: a mod in the cache folder `mods/` loads on the dedicated server with only `Mods=`; the `Mods=`/`WorkshopItems=` format the installer writes (official 42.15 guide: plain MOD_IDs; community sources disagree on a backslash); clients get kicked or warned when files differ; a Workshop-published copy downloads for players on join.
4. **Distribution to players.** Every player needs the same files. The only automatic path is the Steam Workshop, which needs the **creator's own Steam account** (and game licence) to upload; Nxeon cannot upload on a customer's behalf. Owner decision: (a) guide creators to upload via the in-game uploader with a Cyrus-generated `workshop.txt` + preview, or (b) offer "private server pack" downloads that players install by hand. Until then, multiplayer Cyrus mods are only practical for small groups.
5. **Install flow guard.** Nxeon offers PZ variants `b42` (default, stable public branch = 42.21 today) and `b41` (Legacy). Cyrus mods must only install on `b42` servers (lifecycle agent).
6. **Version table maintenance.** On every stable build: read the Steam news feed (app 108600) for "Modding Changelog"/"Migration Guide" posts, re-run the API check against the new JavaDocs, bump `PZ_TARGET.testedOn`, update `versions`, add failure rules. The "Build 42 Support Update" (rest of 2026) promises more modding changes and an official modding guide.
7. **Assets.** Items/vehicles reference icons, models and textures that are not generated; sounds reference `.ogg` clips. `ASSETS.md` lists them. The render/texture plug-in (research agent) would fill this.
8. **Policy.** The Indie Stone's Modding Policy (2.4) forbids selling access to mods. Cyrus can charge for the tool, but the community/mod store must keep Zomboid mods free to download, credit forks (4.1–4.3), and never label a mod "official" (2.2.3). Owner should confirm the community agent's store design respects this.

## Project Zomboid modding in one page (also for the marketing page)

**No loader to install.** Project Zomboid reads mods itself. A mod is a folder with a `mod.info` (id, name, version) and a `media/` folder of Lua scripts and plain-text "script" files that define items, recipes, vehicles and sounds. The game runs Lua 5.1 through Kahlua, a Java implementation, and exposes most of its Java classes to Lua.

**Build 42 is a different game for modders.** Build 42 became the default on 29 July 2026 (42.20; 42.21 is current, Build 41 lives on in the `legacy41` beta). Mods now sit in a version folder (`42/`) next to a `common/` folder for big shared assets; items declare `ItemType = base:weapon`; names, recipes and options are translated through UTF-8 JSON files; tags and weapon categories are registry ids like `base:screwdriver`. Almost every tutorial on the internet is for Build 41, which is why generic AI output breaks here and why Cyrus checks every file against the Build 42 rules first.

**Three Lua folders.** `shared` runs everywhere, `client` on each player's game (UI, keys, what the player sees), `server` on the server (and in singleplayer). Cyrus keeps all game-changing logic on the server: since multiplayer returned in 42.13, items and health that a client changes on its own are thrown away. Players' games detect a trigger and ask the server; the server checks distance, cooldowns and what the player is holding before anything happens.

**Everyone needs the mod.** Unlike a Minecraft plugin, a Zomboid mod runs on the server and on every player's PC, and the files must match. Servers list Workshop ids in `WorkshopItems=` and mod ids in `Mods=`; players then download the mods automatically when they join.

**How mods break.** A new build renames an API (the 42.21 stats system, for example), a Build 41 mod lands on a Build 42 server, two mods ship a file at the same path, or client-side code fights the server. Cyrus pins every mod to a minimum build, uses per-mod folders, puts every number behind a sandbox option with an on/off switch, and flags mods that a new game build may have broken.

# Project Zomboid in Cyrus: readiness checklist and explainer (2026-10-08)

Status: **not live** (`soon`). Flipping it to live is the owner's decision. Branch `feature/cyrus-v6-game-zomboid`.

## What is done

- `lib/cyrus/games/zomboid.ts`: verified GameSupport (versions 42.21 → 41.78, install side `both`, plain-language install text, 17 dangerous-API rules, breakage risks with guards, outdated signals, categories, sources, unknowns) plus a `knowledge` pack (14 API-sheet lines, 12 Build 41→42 failure rules with regex detectors).
- `lib/cyrus/engine/games/zomboid.ts`: the template generator rewritten for Build 42.15+ and the 42.13 multiplayer rules (server-authoritative effects, shared timed actions, JSON translations, `ItemType`/registry ids, own script module, per-mod Lua folders, guarded fire, no map files). API check: `API-CHECK.md`.
- `lib/cyrus/games/zomboid.validate.ts`: static validator (layout, mod.info, Lua 5.1 structure lint written in TypeScript, dangerous APIs, failure rules, MP rules, script braces, JSON translations).
- `test/cyrus-game-zomboid.test.ts`: every category × model × six prompts must pass the validator with zero blocking issues, plus negative tests.

## What is left before it can go live

1. **Real-model generation path.** Today Zomboid output comes from the deterministic template, not from the AI build service (which only builds Minecraft). The live product needs the build service to: take the GameSupport `knowledge` pack as context, generate, run `validateZomboidMod`, feed blocking issues back for repair, and only then show the mod. Owner decision: when to wire it, and whether Zomboid gets its own service endpoint.
2. **Load test in a sandbox (not run).** Needs nothing proprietary in git, but it needs compute:
   - Project Zomboid dedicated server, downloaded by SteamCMD anonymously (app **380870**) inside a throwaway container, the same way Nxeon's own Zomboid image installs it. Nothing is redistributed: Valve's tool fetches it into the sandbox.
   - Steps: copy the mod into `<cachedir>/mods/<ModId>/`, set `Mods=<ModId>` in `Server/servertest.ini`, boot with a fresh world, wait for "SERVER STARTED", run a few game minutes, then grep `console.txt` / `Logs/*DebugLog-server.txt` for `ERROR`, `STACK TRACE`, `attempted index`, `Object tried to call nil` mentioning the mod's files. Exit code + log excerpt = the verdict.
   - Lua unit tests: run the generated busted spec with a free Lua 5.1 (`lua5.1` + `busted`, or the open-source `wasmoon`/`fengari` npm packages). Not installed anywhere today; adding them is a dependency or system-package decision for the owner.
   - Limits: a headless server never runs `lua/client` code, so HUDs, context menus and keybinds still need a human (or a scripted client, which is not available).
   - Resources: about 4 to 6 GB RAM and 2 vCPU per test run (Build 42 is heavy; Nxeon sells 6 GB as the smallest Zomboid plan). Must run on a sandbox VM, never on the build VM or a customer VM.
3. **End-to-end test on a real Nxeon 42.21 server.** Confirm: a mod in the cache folder `mods/` loads on the dedicated server with only `Mods=`; the `Mods=`/`WorkshopItems=` format the installer writes (official 42.15 guide: plain MOD_IDs; community sources disagree on a backslash); clients get kicked or warned when files differ; a Workshop-published copy downloads for players on join.
4. **Distribution to players.** Every player needs the same files. The only automatic path is the Steam Workshop, which needs the **creator's own Steam account** (and game licence) to upload; Nxeon cannot upload on a customer's behalf. Owner decision: (a) guide creators to upload via the in-game uploader with a Cyrus-generated `workshop.txt` + preview, or (b) offer "private server pack" downloads that players install by hand. Until then, multiplayer Cyrus mods are only practical for small groups.
5. **Install flow guard.** Nxeon offers PZ variants `b42` (default, stable public branch = 42.21 today) and `b41` (Legacy). Cyrus mods must only install on `b42` servers (lifecycle agent).
6. **Version table maintenance.** On every stable build: read the Steam news feed (app 108600) for "Modding Changelog"/"Migration Guide" posts, re-run the API check against the new JavaDocs, bump `PZ_TARGET.testedOn`, update `versions`, add failure rules. 7. **Assets.** Items/vehicles reference icons, models and textures that are not generated; sounds reference `.ogg` clips. `ASSETS.md` lists them. The render/texture plug-in (research agent) would fill this.
8. **Policy.** The Indie Stone's Modding Policy (2.4) forbids selling access to mods. Cyrus can charge for the tool, but the community/mod store must keep Zomboid mods free to download, credit forks (4.1–4.3), and never label a mod "official" (2.2.3). Owner should confirm the community agent's store design respects this.

**No loader to install.** Project Zomboid reads mods itself. A mod is a folder with a `mod.info` (id, name, version) and a `media/` folder of Lua scripts and plain-text "script" files that define items, recipes, vehicles and sounds.
